title: Learning in the Age of Algorithmic Video
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick argues that educational video, as students now consume it, has outrun the multimedia-learning research meant to evaluate it: Mayer's principles still hold, but they were established on a learner and a format that no longer exist. Starting from reporting on YouTube saturating school Chromebooks, he surveys how student viewing has changed (speed-watching, captions on by default, second screens, AI summarisers) and how the medium has changed (short-form, algorithmic delivery, AI-generated avatar instructors). He weighs the evidence on each, including a mixed picture on AI offloading where Socratic dialogue helps and summary tools harm, and flags that process claims rest on shaky verbal-report methods. His central design claim is that the unit of analysis is now the learning episode rather than the video, and that embedded prequestions and retrieval prompts are the best-supported defence, alongside conservative coherence choices and AI configured for dialogue rather than delivery. He offers three diagnostic questions for testing any claim to have 'learned so much' from a video, warning of the fluency illusion. He ends with a fair accounting of what such formats do well, such as procedural skills, curiosity and exposure, while insisting these only prepare the ground for learning elsewhere.
points: Mayer's multimedia principles remain sound, but their boundary conditions (single-screen, normal-speed, narrated slides) no longer describe how students actually watch, so designers are designing for a statistically rare learner.

Speed-watching preserves comprehension up to about 2x but degrades metacognitive monitoring, making it worst for material at the edge of a student's schema, which is exactly what instructional video is used for.

AI help in video learning cuts both ways: Socratic, dialogue-style tools help weaker students while summary tools that do the cognitive work harm stronger ones, so an 'ask the AI' button is never pedagogically neutral.
Embedded prequestions and retrieval prompts are named as the single most defensible design lever, backed by the generative-activity principle's large evidence base.
Three questions (what kind of knowledge, what mechanism produced it, what would falsify it) separate genuine learning from the fluency illusion polished videos produce.
quotes: And yet the research we have to make sense of this was conducted on a learner who has since been replaced. Rich Mayer’s seminal work on multimedia theory is some of the most carefully replicated research in educational psychology.
A third paper, from Computers in Human Behavior in early 2025, finds that even where comprehension is preserved, metacognitive monitoring degrades. Students do not know what they are missing.

I see this as a kind of uncanny valley, but one with real pedagogical consequences in the sense that every bit of working memory the brain spends reconciling that incongruity is working memory not available for the actual content.

Taken as a whole, I think the unit of analysis is no longer the video but rather the learning episode. Speed, captions, second screens and AI summarisers all modify the encoding conditions in ways that no scaling of CTML’s principles can fully anticipate.

Embedded prequestions and retrieval prompts convert passive viewing into active engagement at the lowest design cost, and with the strongest empirical base. If I had to pick one design recommendation to defend against everything I have described in this post, that would be it.

One more design heuristic worth naming. AI tools embedded in video learning environments should be configured for dialogue, not for delivery. The empirical pattern is consistent: students who use AI to think (Socratic prompts, follow-up questions, generative tasks) gain; students who use AI to receive (summaries, answers, abridgements) do not.

Educational video, in the form most students now consume it, has run ahead of the science designed to evaluate it. The field is in roughly the position medicine would be in if the only randomised trials had been conducted on a population that no longer existed. The principles are good. The patient has changed.
